title: Atomic nickel cluster decorated defect-rich copper for enhanced C2 product selectivity in electrocatalytic CO2 reduction
abstract: This work describes a coordination enabled galvanic replacement method to decorate atomic Ni clusters on defect-rich Cu surface to provide the first Ni/Cu bimetallic system that significantly enhances the production of C2 products from electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. Specifically, with a surface Ni/Cu ratio of 0.82 %, a 7-fold increase in the selectivity for C2 products was found in comparison with pristine Cu. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the rate determining step for *CO formation changes from the formation of *COOH on copper to the chemisorption of CO2 on Ni decorated surfaces. An alteration of binding sites from Ni-Ni bridge for *CO2 and *COOH to Ni-Cu bridge for *CO is discovered and is proposed to favor the key C–C coupling step. The catalytic mechanism demonstrated in the Cu-Ni system points to the new directions for the development of advanced bimetallic electrocatalysts for producing multi-carbon materials from CO2 reduction.

Atomic nickel cluster decorated defect-rich copper for enhanced C2 product selectivity in electrocatalytic CO2 reduction
Xiaolong Zhang a,1, Chuangwei Liu a,1, Yong Zhao c, Linbo Li a, Yu Chen d, Fazal Raziq e, Liang Qiao e, Si-Xuan Guo a,b, Caiyun Wang c, Gordon G. Wallace c, Alan M. Keywords: Carbon dioxide reduction Electrocatalysis Bimetallic catalyst Surface decoration
A B S T R A C T
This work describes a coordination enabled galvanic replacement method to decorate atomic Ni clusters on defect-rich Cu surface to provide the first Ni/Cu bimetallic system that significantly enhances the production of C2 products from electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. Specifically, with a surface Ni/Cu ratio of 0.82 %, a 7-fold increase in the selectivity for C2 products was found in comparison with pristine Cu. Density functional theory calculations reveal that the rate determining step for *CO formation changes from the formation of *COOH on copper to the chemisorption of CO2 on Ni decorated surfaces. An alteration of binding sites from Ni-Ni bridge for *CO2 and *COOH to Ni-Cu bridge for *CO is discovered and is proposed to favor the key C–C coupling step. The catalytic mechanism demonstrated in the Cu-Ni system points to the new directions for the development of advanced bimetallic electrocatalysts for producing multi-carbon materials from CO2 reduction.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Electrocatalytic conversion of CO2 into value-added chemical feedstocks and fuels using renewable electricity is an attractive pathway towards a closed anthropogenic carbon cycle and a net-zero carbon economy [1–3]. Consequently, both fundamental and applied aspects of the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (eCO2RR) has been widely explored in recent years [4–6]. Highly efficient electrocatalysts for the production of simple C1 products such as carbon monoxide (CO) [7–9] and formic acid (HCOOH) have been frequently reported [10–13]. However, selective production of more highly reduced hydrocarbons and oxygenates, especially C2 products, with higher value and energy densities, remains challenging due to the limited activity, selectivity or long term stability of presently available electrocatalysts [14,15].
To date, Cu-based materials are the most capable catalysts for reducing CO2 to a wide range of hydrocarbon and oxygenate products with decent efficiencies [16]. The unique feature of Cu arises from its
intermediate binding strength to CO, which is one of the key factors determining the performance of an electrocatalyst [17,18]. However, pristine Cu electrocatalysts suffer from low product selectivity with at least 16 products detected [19]. To overcome this drawback, Cu-based electrocatalysts should be rationally designed to break the scaling relationship, thereby allowing the adsorption energy of a particular intermediate to be optimized in order to facilitate selective production of a desired product [2,20]. An effective strategy to break the scaling relationship is to introduce a second metal into Cu. A few studies have reported improved eCO2RR selectivity and efficiency towards C2+ (products containing at least two carbons) products on Cu-based bimetallic materials, such as Cu-Ag [21,22] and Cu-Au [23]. This kind of binary materials could be designed to have catalytic sites with tuned binding energies and/or configurations for key reaction intermediates [24].
Ni is another metal that is capable of reducing CO2 to hydrocarbons, albeit only with very low faradaic efficiencies at high overpotentials

[25]. Strong binding of CO to Ni leads to the poisoning of the Ni surface. Turning Ni material into single atom forms or alloying it with other metals can effectively destabilize the Ni-CO interaction. For instance, coordinatively unsaturated single atom Ni sites supported on nitrogen-doped carbon exhibits a high CO production rate at a low overpotential and NiGa alloy greatly improves the yields of highly reduced products [26–28]. Due to the stronger CO affinity to Ni than Cu, the presence of Ni on a Cu surface could potentially increase the coverage of CO at low overpotential, thus enhancing the kinetics of the rate determining C–C coupling process, and favoring the formation of C2 products. However, the Cu-Ni alloys explored for eCO2RR so far only show improved selectivity towards C1 products [29,30]. The surface segregation tendency of Ni in such alloys results in non-uniform distribution of Ni, which diminishes the advantages of such a bimetallic system [31]. We therefore reason that Ni, if highly dispersed on the Cu surface, could be more efficient in enhancing C–C coupling and promoting the production of multi carbon products. However, the challenge lies in the synthesis of highly dispersed Ni on a Cu surface. It is difficult to generate such a structure from two metals that are vastly different in physicochemical properties such as redox potential and melting point [32]. Here we report a coordination enabled galvanic replacement method that can achieve uniform dispersion of atomic Ni clusters on the surface of a defect-rich Cu nanowire. A 7-fold increase in the selectivity of C2 products was found on the Ni decorated sample in comparison with non-decorated Cu.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials and apparatus
sections.text:
Nickel nitrate (Ni(NO3)2∙6H2O, 98 %), sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3), hydrochloric acid (HCl, 32 %), toluene (anhydrous, 99.8 %) and sulfur powder (reagent grade) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Acetonitrile (anhydrous, 99.9 %) was purchased from Merck. Copper foam (99.9 %, 110 PPI) was purchased from Suzhou Jiashide Metal Foam Co. Ltd., China. Pressurized CO2 cylinder (Food Grade) was supplied by Air Liquide. All chemicals were used as supplied. All aqueous solutions were prepared with deionized water produced in a MilliQMilliRho purification system.
A JEOL 7001 F instrument was used to collect scanning electron microscopic (SEM) images. A Bruker D8 Eco powder diffractometer was used to record powder X-ray Diffraction (XRD) data. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was performed using a Nexsa surface analysis system (Thermofisher). A FEI Tecnai G2 T20 TWIN TEM instrument was used to collect transmission electron microscopic (TEM) images. A FEI Tecnai G2 F20 S-TWIN FEGTEM instrument was used to collect high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images and energy-dispersive X-ray spectra (EDS). Atomic-resolution HAADF-STEM images were taken using a spherical aberration corrected FEI Titan G3 60–300 kV TEM/STEM microscope at 300 kV. A Bruker DRX400 spectrometer was used for 1H NMR experiments. An Agilent 7820A gas chromatography (GC) instrument equipped with a Flame Ionization Detector (FID) and a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) was used to quantify gaseous electrolysis products.

sections.heading: 2.2.1. Synthesis of Cu foam@Cu1.8S
sections.text: A piece of Cu foam (1 × 3 cm2) was cleaned in acetone and then in a 1.0 M HCl aqueous solution by ultrasonication for 10 min. The cleaned Cu foam was rinsed with acetone, and then immersed immediately into a 20 mL sulphur saturated toluene solution. After 1 min, the colour of the Cu foam turned black. At this stage, the black Cu foam was removed from the toluene solution and rinsed with acetone to obtain Cu foam@Cu1.8S.

sections.heading: 2.2.2. Preparation of Cu nanowire (CuNW) and Ni decorated Cu nanowire (Ni-CuNW)
sections.text:
CuNW was obtained by the electrochemical reduction of Cu foam@Cu1.8S in 0.50 M sodium bicarbonate solution at -1.0 V vs Ag/ AgCl for 30 min. A piece of Cu foam@Cu1.8S was used as the working electrode in a three-electrode electrochemical system, with graphite rod and Ag/AgCl (3.0 M KCl) as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. The as-obtained CuNW was then rinsed with water, ethanol and acetone, consecutively, and dried in a dry box under a N2 atmosphere.
Ni decoration was achieved by immersing the freshly prepared CuNW into a 50 mL acetonitrile solution containing 50 mM Ni(NO3)2 for 0.5, 1, 2, or 5 min. The as-obtained Ni-CuNW was then rinsed with acetone and dried under a N2 atmosphere at room temperature.

sections.heading: 2.2.3. Fabrication of gas diffusion electrodes
sections.text: To fabricate gas diffusion electrodes, CuNW or Ni-CuNW were first peeled off from the Cu foam substrate by ultrasonication. Then 20 mg of the as-obtained CuNW or Ni-CuNW was mixed with 2 mL iso-propanol and 30 μL 5% Nafion solution to form a catalyst ink. An aliquot of the catalyst ink (100 μL) was dropcast evenly on the surface of a carbon paper (1.5 × 1.5 cm2) with a microporous carbon black layer containing Vulcan XC72R carbon black (~0.9 mg cm− 2) and polytetrafluoroethylene (~15 wt%). The electrode was then left at room temperature for 10 min and subsequently at 70 ◦C for 30 min to evaporate the solvent. The catalyst loading is approximately 0.44 mg cm− 2.

sections.heading: 2.3.1. Experiments conducted with an H-type cell
sections.text: A CHI700D electrochemical workstation (CHI Instruments, USA) was used for all electrochemical experiments. The Cu foam supported CuNW or Ni-CuNW were directly used as the working electrodes. Ag/AgCl (1.0 M KCl) was used as the reference electrode. A graphite rod was used as the counter electrode. The experimentally measured potentials were later converted to the RHE scale using the formula: ERHE = EAg/AgCl + 0.190 + 0.0586 × pH. A gas tight two-compartment H-cell was used for bulk electrolysis. A porous glass frit was used to separate the anolyte and catholyte. The electrolyte was bubbled with high purity CO2 gas for 20 min prior to electrochemical measurements. All electrochemical experiments were performed at room temperature (22 ± 1 ◦C).

sections.heading: 2.3.2. Experiments conducted with a gas diffusion flow cell system
sections.text: A custom-made three-channel flow cell was employed for further investigation of the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction performance of the materials. The electrode working area was 1.0 cm2 and the distance between electrode and membrane was 1.0 cm. The Hg/HgO (1.0 M KOH) reference electrode (BASi) was located ~ 1 cm from the cathode. Conversion of all experimentally measured potentials to the RHE scale was undertaken using the formula: ERHE = EHg/HgO + 0.0586 × pH + Ru × I, where Ru is the recorded resistance of the system and I is the magnitude of the recorded current. A mass flow controller (GFC17, Aalborg®) was used to control the gas flow rate (40 ccm) into the flow cell. A peristaltic pump (Longer Pump, BT100-2 J) was used to control the catholyte flow rates, with a catholyte flow rate of 20 mL min− 1. The anolyte flow rate was 20 mL min− 1. A 1.0 M KOH solution was used as the electrolyte medium. An anion exchange membrane (Sustainion® 37–50, Dioxide Materials) was used to separate the catholyte and the anolyte.

sections.heading: 2.4. Analysis of the electrolysis products
sections.text:
For electrolysis experiments conducted with an H-cell, offline GC was used to detect gaseous products in the headspace of the cathode compartment. Calibration curves for H2, CO, CH4 and C2H4 were obtained by injecting known amounts of the corresponding standard gas
X. Zhang et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 291 (2021) 120030
into GC. The as-obtained peak area was then plotted as a function of the amount of the standard gas injected. 1H NMR spectrometry was employed to quantify the liquid product(s). Typically, 500 μL of electrolyte solution after electrolysis was mixed with 100 μL DMSO/H2O (1/ 1000 by volume) and 100 μL D2O, where DMSO was used as an internal standard and D2O as a deuterium source.
For electrolysis experiments conducted with a gas diffusion electrode in a flow cell, gas products were analyzed on a Multigas #3 GC (SRI Instruments) equipped with a HayeSep D and Molsieve 5Å columns connected to a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a flame ionization detector (FID). H2 was detected with the TCD, while CO, CH4 and C2H4 were detected with both FID and TCD. A standard gas mixture composed of H2, CO, CH4, C2H4 and CO2 (BOC Australia) was used to obtain the calibration curve for the quantification of each component. Liquid products were quantified following a similar procedure used for the detection of liquid products in an H-type cell.

sections.heading: 2.5. DFT calculations
sections.text: All the computations in this work were based on the standard Density Functional Theory (DFT) using Vienna ab initio Simulation Package (5.4.4 VASP) [33]. Generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) was used to treat the electron exchange correlation functional [34]. The electron–ion interactions was described by the projector-augmented wave method and the cut-off energy for the plane–wave basis set was 500 eV. 3 × 3×1 k-points using the Monkhorst-Pack scheme grid for geometry optimization and self-consistent calculations were used to sample the Brillouin zone. A 3 × 3×1 supercell of Cu (111) with four layers was used to model the electrochemical interface, having two lower layers fixed and the two upper layers relaxed. The maximum force on each atom was lower than -0.02 eV/A and 10− 5 eV to fully relax the atomic position. To avoid interaction between two periodic units, a vacuum space exceeding 15 Å was employed. The zero-point and thermal energy corrections were calculated over Γ points [35]. Spin polarization of the valence state has been taken into account in all calculations. The transition states were calculated with the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method [36]. Forces on the climbing image were converged to less than 0.03 eV/Å. The same cutoff, functional, and calculator parameters as those used in the geometry optimizations were applied.

sections.heading: 3.1. Catalyst preparation and characterization
sections.text:
The standard reduction potential (Eo) for the Ni2+/Ni couple (Eq. 1) is much lower than that of Cu+/Cu (Eq. 2) or Cu2+/Cu (Eq. 3). Therefore, direct galvanic replacement of Cu with Ni2+ is not feasible. In principle, Cu can be electroplated with Ni. However, it is difficult to achieve uniform dispersion of atomic Ni clusters on the surface of Cu using the electroplating method. It is well-known that the coordinatively unsaturated adatoms are electrochemically far less stable than the bulk counterparts [37]. Therefore, the galvanic replacement of Cu adatoms by Ni2+ may proceed on a defect-rich Cu substrate. If it does occur, a uniform distribution of Ni atoms on the surface of Cu may be expected since replacement of bulk Cu by Ni2+ is not thermodynamically favorable as discussed above.
Ni 2+ + 2e− ⇌ Ni (s) E0 = − 0.236 V (1)
Cu+ + e− ⇌ Cu (s) E0 = 0.518 V (2)
Cu2+ + 2e− ⇌ Cu (s) E0 = 0.339 V (3)
In order to prepare a defect-rich Cu surface, a copper sulfide layer coated metallic Cu substrate was first synthesized, which can then be
reduced electrochemically to generate metallic copper materials with an abundance of coordinatively unsaturated sites on the surface [38]. Using Cu foam as the substrate to achieve a large catalytic active site density, a simple room temperature solution based sulfidation process was used to synthesize copper sulfide coated Cu. The as-prepared copper sulfide coated Cu foam shows a compact surface layer with a thickness of 3.5 μm (Fig. S1a–c, ESI). The X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern (Fig. S1d, ESI) obtained on the copper sulfide coated Cu foam matches well with that of the standard Cu1.8S (JCPDS no. 92-1966). The as-obtained copper sulfide coated Cu foam is therefore denoted as Cu foam@Cu1.8S. The sulfide layer was then electrochemically reduced to metallic Cu in an aqueous 0.50 M NaHCO3 medium at -1.0 V vs. Ag/AgCl, as confirmed by powder XRD (Fig. 1a). Two weak diffraction peaks ascribed to CuO, that result from the oxidation of the sulfide derived Cu in air during sample transfer, are also present in the XRD patterns. The sulfide derived Cu shows a highly porous nanowire morphology (Fig. 1b). Those nanowires are formed following an anisotropic growth mechanism proposed previously [39]. The sulfidation process creates trenches on the Cu substrate. During the electrochemical reduction of the sulfide layer, the electrogenerated Cu atoms first enter the trenches through surface diffusion, followed by anisotropic growth to form CuNWs. Under high magnification scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Fig. 1c), the CuNW shows an enriched hierarchical structure. More interestingly, a high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image (Fig. 1d) shows the surface of the CuNW is composed of nano grains with mismatched lattice directions, indicating a defect-rich surface with numerous grain boundaries. This provides a highly active surface for the decaration of Ni atoms in the following step.
The freshly synthesized CuNW was rinsed with water and ethanol under N2 protection, and then immediately immersed into a N2 saturated aqueous solution containing 50 mM Ni(NO3)2. However, no galvanic replacement reaction takes place between the surface Cu adatoms and Ni2+ in the solution. Our group has previously reported the coating of Cu with Bi using a coordination enabled galvanic replacement method [39]. The principle of this method is based on the fact that the reduction potential of Cu+ to Cu could be reduced by more than 0.5 V in the presence of nitrile ligands, such as acetonitrile (Eq. 4), so that a spontaneous galvanic replacement of Cu by the ion of a more reactive metal becomes possible.
[Cu(MeCN)4]+ + e− ⇌ Cu (s) + 4 MeCN E0 = − 0. 048 V (4)
Indeed, when the freshly prepared CuNW was immersed into an acetonitrile solution containing 50 mM Ni(NO3)2 for 1 min, the galvanic reaction took place. The as-obtained Ni-CuNW retains the morphology of CuNW, as shown in the TEM image (Fig. 2a). The presence of Ni on the Ni-CuNW was unambiguously verified by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) analysis in combination with high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) (Fig. 2b). The elemental composition distribution on Ni-CuNW is shown in Fig. 2c. It is clear that Ni is uniformly dispersed on the surface of Cu nanowires although lateral growth of surface Ni ensembles may be expected given a drastic difference in the physicochemical properties of Cu and Ni. Trace amount of residual sulfur was also detected in Ni-CuNW. The surface atomic structures of CuNW and Ni-CuNW are shown in the aberration-corrected bright-field (BF) STEM images in Fig. 2d and e, respectively. Both surfaces have the characteristics of a Cu (111) surface. Since the atomic numbers of Cu and Ni are very similar, no strong contrast in the STEM image of those two atoms is expected. However, isolated regions with slightly lower contrast were found on the Ni-CuNW surface, as marked by red arrows in Fig. 2e. Although it is hard to define the boundaries of these isolated regions, most of them consist of far less than 10 atoms (or < 1 nm). This size is at least an order of magnitude smaller than that obtained by conventional electroplating [40]. The BF-STEM images obtained on the other Ni-CuNW samples show a positive correlation between the size of the surface isolated regions and the
X. Zhang et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 291 (2021) 120030
reaction time (Fig. S2, ESI). Such surface structures are uniformly distributed on the surface of Ni-CuNW but were not found on CuNW. This feature, in combination with the EDX mapping results, suggests that the isolated regions are the surface decorated Ni clusters.
The Ni-Cu ratio on the surface of Ni-CuNW was determined using XPS. The surface chemical compositions determined are summarized in Table S1. Residual amounts of N, S, and Na resulting from the materials preparation procedure were observed. Significant amounts of C and O were also detected, which were from the carbon tape used to fix the powder samples. Fig. 2f provides a plot of the Ni-Cu ratio as a function of reaction time. Clearly, the ratio is positively correlated with the reaction time, but gradually reaches a maximum value after 2 min. The surface Ni atom% at reaction times of 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 5.0 min are 0.13 %, 0.82 %, 1.3 %, and 1.5 %, respectively. For convenience of presentation, these four Ni-CuNW samples are denoted as CuNi-1, CuNi-2, CuNi-3, and CuNi-4, respectively. Fig. 2g shows the core-level Cu 2p XPS spectra of the CuNW and Ni-CuNW samples. Overall, the intensity of the Cu 2p peaks decreases in the order CuNi-1 > CuNi-2 > CuNi-3 > CuNi-4. The Cu 2p XPS spectrum of the CuNW contains the characteristics Cu 2p peaks of CuO with two strong satellite peaks (Cu 2p1/2, sat and Cu 2p3/2, sat) [41], indicating that the sample surface is partially oxidized, most likely by air during sample transfer. The XPS spectrum of CuNi-1 is very similar to that of CuNW except that a shoulder was observed at 932.3 eV. This shoulder gradually becomes a major peak in the XPS spectra of CuNi-2, CuNi-3 and CuNi-4. This peak is related to the d-electron interaction between Cu and Ni, which is often observed in CuNi alloys [42]. However, as Ni only exists on the surface of Cu, CuNi samples samples do not fall under the typical catagory of an alloy. Such structures should be regarded as surface doping with strong bonding interaction. No peaks associated with CuO were found due to the presence of more reactive Ni which prevents the occurrence of Cu oxidation, as has been observed in the case of CuNi anti-corrosion alloys [43]. Fig. 2h shows the spectra of the Cu Auger region. The indicated binding energies are associated with L2M4,5M4,5 (565.2 eV) and L3M4,5M4,5 (568.0 eV) arising from Cu(0). The increasing intensity of the Cu(0) Auger peak in the presence of a higher surface Ni content indicates a greater ratio of Cu
(0) to other Cu species. On the other hand, all the Ni 2p XPS spectra (Fig. 2i) are associated with NiO. The surface Ni clusters are so reactive that they are oxidized instantly when exposed to air during sample transfer. These peak intensities increase in the order of CuNi-1 < CuNi-2 < CuNi-3 < CuNi-4, consistent with an increasing surface Ni content.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction performance
sections.text:
The eCO2RR activity and product selectivity of CuNWs and NiCuNWs were examined in a two-compartment H-cell with a CO2 saturated 0.50 M NaHCO3 aqueous solution (pH 7.2) as the electrolyte medium. The eCO2RR was undertaken in the potential range of –0.56 V to –1.06 V vs. RHE. Faradaic efficiency (FE) distributions for each product obtained with CuNW, CuNi-1, CuNi-2 and CuNi-3 are presented in Fig. 3a–d and Tables S2–S5. The total FEs in all cases are close to 100 %. For CuNW, the FEs for H2 are over 49 % under all applied potentials and formate is the main CO2 reduction product. Small amounts of C2 products were detected at potentials more negative than more negative -0.67 V vs. RHE. Production of H2 was significantly suppressed in the case of both CuNi-1 and CuNi-2. For CuNi-2, the lowest FE for H2 of 17 % was obtained at -0.87 V vs. RHE and significant amounts of C2 products were detected at potentials more negative than -0.67 V vs. RHE. The highest FE for C2H5OH was 16 % obtained at -0.77 V vs. RHE while that for C2H4 of 24 % was obtained at -0.97 V vs. RHE. Evidently, when CuNW is decorated with a small amount of Ni, the kinetics of the rate determining C–C coupling step is greatly enhanced. However, the CO2 reduction performance of the Ni-CuNW catalysts depends on the Ni content on the Cu surface. CuNi-1 exhibited only a slightly higher selectivity towards C2 products than that of CuNW but much lower than that of CuNi-2, while CuNi-3 mainly produces H2 with a FE of over 81 % under all applied potentials. Fig. 3e shows the comparison of the overall faradaic efficiency for C2+ products (FEC2+) on CuNW and Ni-CuNW catalysts. CuNi2 exhibits the highest selectivity towards C2 products under all applied potentials. At -0.77 V vs. RHE, the FEC2+ on CuNi-2 is 44 %, which is about 7-fold higher than that on CuNW (6.3 %). It should be noted that Ni decoration on CuNW does not introduce a significant change in the
X. Zhang et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 291 (2021) 120030
electroactive surface area, since similar electrochemical double layer capacitance values were obtained on the CuNW and Ni-CuNW samples (Fig. S3, ESI). The enhanced C2+ selectivity is therefore attributed to the intrinsic properties of the catalyst, to be discussed in detail later. The CuNi-2 catalyst also exhibited a stable catalytic current density of ~ 18 mA cm− 2 at -0.86 V vs. RHE over a 6 h electrolysis experiment with FEC2 retained around 40 % (Fig. 3f). After the long-term electrolysis, the Cu 2p XPS spectrum (Fig. S4a, ESI) of the CuNi-2 catalyst shows strong characteristics of metallic Cu. In contrast, the Ni 2p XPS spectrum (Fig. S4b, ESI) remains similar to that found before electrolysis. The detected Ni atom% was 0.78 %, which was close to the value of 0.82 % found before electrolysis. Also, no significant change in the CuNi-2 morphology was observed by TEM after long term electrolysis (Fig. S4c, d, ESI). The high physical and chemical stability of the CuNi-2 catalyst therefore leads to the high catalytic stability.
The eCO2RR performance of CuNW and CuNi-2 catalysts was further investigated in a flow cell electrolyzer, which is composed of a gas diffusion electrode, two compartments for liquid electrolytes, and one gas compartment for CO2 delivery and gas product collection. The cell and the gas diffusion layer (GDL) were designed according to previous reports [44–46]. A 1.0 M KOH solution was used as the electrolyte medium, as a previous study suggests that OH− ions on or near the Cu
surface can lower the CO2 reduction and CO–CO coupling activation energy barriers [47]. It should be noted though, that the long-term stability test in such an alkaline flow cell system is problematic due to the reaction between OH− and CO2. Significantly enhanced catalytic current density was obtained in the flow cell system where the mass transport rate is much higher, as shown in Fig. 4a. All potentials reported in these experiments have been corrected for the uncompensated resistance effect (IRu). The current density recorded on the CuNi-2 sample is larger than that of CuNW at applied potentials more negative than -0.60 V vs. RHE. Considering that the electroactive surface area of the two samples are similar, it is concluded that the CuNi-2 shows higher catalytic activity than CuNW under these conditions. CuNi-2 also shows much higher FEC2+ than CuNW under all applied potentials (Fig. 4b), which further confirms that Ni decoration on CuNW can facilitate the formation of multi-carbon products. It is postulated that the presence of Ni on the Cu surface enhances the coverage of *CO (* represents an adsorption site) due to the strong CO affinity to Ni. Furthermore, previous studies have found that the surface coordinatively unsaturated Cu atoms actually accelerate the hydrogen evolution reaction and the CO2 reduction to CO instead of the subsequent hydrogenation of CO [48]. Thus, partial replacement of surface coordination unsaturated Cu atoms by Ni atoms contributes to the enhanced multi-carbon product
X. Zhang et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 291 (2021) 120030
selectivity. Both CuNW and CuNi-2 showed significantly improved selectivity towards C2+ products compared with the results obtained under the Hcell conditions. For CuNW (Table S6), the production of H2 has been largely suppressed, with the lowest FEH2 of 31 % at -0.70 V vs. RHE. Although formate was still the dominant CO2 reduction product, the selectivity towards C2 products was about twice that obtained in the Hcell. Even a small amount of propanol was detected. For CuNi-2 (Table S7), the FEH2 values obtained under all applied potentials were below 21 %, while the highest FEC2+ value of 62 % (including 5% propanol) was obtained at an applied potential of -0.88 V vs. RHE, which is about 50 % higher than that obtained at a similar potential in an Hcell. When compared to literature data (Table S8), other Ni/Cu bimetallic systems [29] only achieve promotion of C1 products. The CuNi catalyst herein is the first Ni/Cu bimetallic catalyst that can significantly enhance the production of C2 products. It also shows a comparable C2 products formation rate to that of the state-of-the-art Cu based bimetallic catalysts, albeit the selectivity towards a specific C2 product needs to be further improved in future work.

sections.heading: 3.3. Mechanistic study
sections.text:
In order to investigate the role played by Ni atoms in the Cu-Ni samples, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to reveal the CO2 catalytic mechanism on eight possible model structures (Fig. S5, ESI) with different number of Ni atoms (0~7) decorated on the Cu (111) surface. The Ni doping levels corresponding to 0~2.0 Ni atom% in four layers of Cu atoms. Each model of Ni decorated Cu is named xNi, where x is the number of Ni substitutes. Initially, three key C1 intermediates *CO2, *COOH and *CO, were studied on different catalytic sites, including Cu, Ni, Cu-Ni bridge, and Ni-Ni bridge (Figs. 5a and S6, ESI). The results indicated that the Ni decoration significantly decrease the energy barrier for all three intermediates. The step with the highest energy barrier switched from the formation of *COOH on a Cu surface to the formation of *CO2 on the Ni decorated Cu surfaces. This suggests that the chemisorption of CO2 is the rate determining step (RDS) for CO2 reduction to *CO on the Ni decorated Cu surfaces. More significantly, the CO2 adsorption and hydrogenation to form *COOH are preferred on the Ni-Ni bridge, while further hydrogenation occurs at CuNi bridge to form *CO (Fig. 5b). This could lead to local accumulation of
X. Zhang et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 291 (2021) 120030
*CO and favor the follow-up dimerization reaction on the Cu sites [49]. The residual sulfur is not considered here, as previous studies have shown that sulfur atoms in sulfide derived Cu can only promote the production of formate by stabilizing the *OCOH intermediate [38,50]. Furthermore, since all our samples contain trace sulfur, enhanced C2 product selectivity associated with Ni-CuNW is therefore attributed to the Ni content.
To further clarify the relationship between catalytic performance and the doping concentration, the maximum Gibbs free energy (ΔG*CO2) is plotted as a function of the Ni substitute number on a Cu surface in Fig. 5c. Interestingly, ΔG*CO2 decreases upon increasing the Ni substitution at first, reaching the lowest ΔG*CO2 at 3Ni. Further increase in the Ni substitute number increases ΔG*CO2. This provides an explanation for the volcano-like trend of the catalytic activity for the eCO2RR with respect to the Ni content observed experimentally. Importantly, the Ni doping level of 0.87 % for the 3Ni model is close to that of 0.82 % found in the best performing CuNi-2 sample. Therefore, the dimerization reaction, a key step for C2 production, was further investigated on the 3Nidecorated Cu (111) surface by DFT calculations. The barrier for coupling between CO adsorbates was determined using nudged elastic band calculations and was found to be 0.94 eV (Fig. 5d), which is lower than the value of 1.5 eV at pristine Cu electrodes [51]. The structures of the initial and final transition state adsorbates are shown in Fig. 5e. It is found that the final adsorbate C2O2* binds to three Cu atoms through both O and C, which is consistent with the results reported by Calle-Vallejo and Koper [52]. The Bader charge analysis suggests that the neighboring Cu obtains extra electron from Ni, which decreases the kinetic barrier for C–C coupling. Using the computational hydrogen electrode approach and the same charged solvation environment used for the dimer, it is found that HOCCO* is the most favorable intermediate from the hydrogenation of CO-dimer. The possible energy profiles for ethanol and ethylene formation via concerted proton-electron transfer pathways are illustrated in Fig. S7, ESI. It can be seen that most of the steps are exothermic and proceed by hydrogenation of the C moieties. Notably, the selectivity between ethylene and ethanol is determined by the tendency for deoxygenation of *OCHCH2. Our calculation results reveal that the
deoxygenation of *OCHCH2 to form ethylene (0.22 eV) is slightly more favorable than further hydrogenation to form ethanol (0.58 eV), which is consistent with the observation of ethylene as the main C2 product in our experiments.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
We have developed a coordination enabled galvanic replacement method to achieve the uniform decoration of atomic Ni clusters on a defect-rich copper surface. We have demonstrated for the first time that nickel decoration on copper could significantly enhance the production of C2 products from the eCO2RR. The catalytic performance of such nickel decorated Cu was highly surface component sensitive. Under an optimum condition with a surface Ni/Cu ratio of 0.82 %, a 7-fold increase in the selectivity for C2 products was found in comparison with pristine Cu. A maximum FE of 62 % for C2+ products was obtained at -0.88 V vs. RHE in a flow cell with an alkaline 1.0 M KOH electrolyte. DFT calculations revealed that decoration of Ni atoms significantly decreased the energy barrier for all C1 intermediates. The RDS changed from the formation of *COOH on copper to the chemisorption of CO2 on Ni decorated Cu surfaces. A strong correlation between the maximum Gibbs free energy of *CO2 and the eCO2RR activity is verified. More interestingly, a change of the binding sites from the Ni-Ni bridge for *CO2 and *COOH to the Ni-Cu bridge for *CO was discovered and was proposed to favor the C–C coupling step. Reaction pathways for the formation of ethylene and ethanol from *CO− CO also were analyzed by the DFT calculations. The result indicated that HOCCO* was the most favorable intermediate from the hydrogenation of CO-dimer, and the deoxygenation of *OCHCH2 to form ethylene was slightly more favorable than further hydrogenation to form ethanol. We expect that the ratio of the C2 products could be further tuned by controlling the oxygen affinity of the copper surface. This work provides motivation for further investigation of non-precious metal-copper bimetallic systems for the production of value-added multi-carbon products from electrocatalytic CO2 reduction.
